utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. While we're waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, Mr. Lukic, and I'm addressing lead counsel at this moment, the Chamber is still in some uncertainty about the witnesses to that will appear this week. Especially in view of the videolink, we'd like to know as soon as possible what we could expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I think I can already answer your question. We have a witness who is coming tonight, but we will not be able to put him on stand tomorrow morning since we have to see him first, so probably we will have nobody for Tuesday but we will proceed on Wednesday with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that will be Mr. Kenic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. That's the only thing you have. Good morning, Mr. Tusevljak. Not very polite of us to continue to deal with out matters when you entered the courtroom, but [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Lukic, you may continue. However, my time records tells me that where you say you would need one and a half to two hours, that you're four minutes off from two hours which is pretty close. So, therefore, do your best. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Thursday, we stopped at video 1D6006C. Since there was this small omission on my part, I would like to ask that the video be played again, 1D06006C.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... since we didn't verify this -- the transcripts for this video, we should play it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the second time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] It's been 12 days since the Muslim offensive and the general emergency signal is continuously on. Everyday the enemy fires several missiles indiscriminately on this urban part of Srpsko Sarajevo and covers with machine-gun and sniper fire all the streets, intersections and alleys within sight. "Bogoljub Usorac: Snipers are the most dangerous, especially those from the faculty over there. You cannot pass there. They are constantly firing. "Dragan Konic: We can't move one bit because of the snipers. Shells are fired from all sides. Two days ago, a woman got killed here. A child was wounded there. There, on that balcony, a child was wounded. Also a woman was wounded there. That woman was seriously wounded and she succumbed to the injury. Another man who was standing there when that shell exploded. He was wounded there. You know, it was horrible. Terrible what they do. They don't choose."

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw the last interlocutor. We see what he said about how Grbavica was fired at. From the place where the other interlocutor was standing in this interview, how far away are enemy front lines from that particular place, the closest ones.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 200 to 300 metres roughly, not more than 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which buildings are the most dominant in that part of enemy territory facing Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the side where the Muslim forces were, it was the faculty of mechanical engineering that was dominant and the Bristol hotel and the building of the joint organs of the current Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the Executive Council of the then-Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge and recollection, what was being used to fire at the population of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the investigation that was carried out by the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska or, rather, the team that I headed, in that period of time during 1992 up until the end of 1993, in the area of Grbavica about 700 civilians were killed. They were either killed from fire-arms - that is to say, infantry weapons - or they were victims of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know from which buildings they attacked in this way that you described to us?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it was possible to carry out an on-site investigation, a particular process was carried out. That is to say, establishing the place from which the firing had come. As I already mentioned these facilities were the places from which Grbavica was being fired at most of the time. I'm speaking about infantry weapons. And also Golubovo Brdo was fired from as well. It was on the slopes of Mount Trebevic and Grbavica could be seen without any obstacles. And also firing came from the so-called Sanac, which is on the slopes of Mojmilo hill from where Grbavica could also be seen clearly without a single obstacle in sight. These are the locations from which most of the firing against Grbavica took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please move a bit away from the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you move a tiny little bit away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said, this is the urban part of the city of Sarajevo and it is mostly civilians that live there. The lines were in front and behind there were civilians who lived there, and they were a target of attacks very often. Because when the distances are so small, speaking of infantry fire, the marksmen could very clearly make a distinction between civilians and members of the Army of Republika Srpska. When I talked to you about these casualties over 700, in that period when, in Grbavica up until the end of 1993, 1.600 people were killed. But this number in terms of the difference in respect of fatalities that is, these are members of the Army of Republika Srpska so we didn't take that into account when we were trying to calculate the number of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that from that distance a clear distinction could be made between civilians and soldiers. Apart from civilians and soldiers, who else were the victims of such attacks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very often children were the victims of these attacks. We have many such examples of on-site investigations, video footage, photographs where killed children can be seen. Children who were 10, 12, 13, so visually and in terms of their height, one could ascertain that they were children, so the people who were doing the shooting could see that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like call 65 ter 1D06007a. Since we didn't verify the transcripts for this video with CLSS, we need to play this video twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton, one question: We heard now evidence that civilians on the Serbian side fell victim to sniping and also to shelling. Is that in dispute that such victims fell?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh we've -- no, Your Honour. Of course, [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why are we hearing evidence on matters which are not in dispute, Mr. Lukic. I waited for a while, listened, and I never gained the idea that the Prosecution says there is no sniping and no shelling in Sarajevo and that, of course, victim, civilian victims fell on the other side as well. Why do we have to hear it?

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our intention is to prove that enemy soldiers from the territory controlled by the BH army were firing from civilian buildings that did not have a military purpose but they turned it into facilities with a military purpose and from there, they were firing at civilian areas of Sarajevo that were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. Of course, they had to be neutralised by the army in order to protect the population. We are trying that show that actually these buildings were a legitimate military objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether they will be, yes or no, is another matter. But then please focus on that. Please, then, focus in detail on where this sniping incident, from where it was shot, et cetera, rather than showing running children, which, of course, if you snipe at civilians, people will start running. That's -- but let's then focus on what you want to establish and then we'll further see. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can play the video now.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have a wrong video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that you asked for 1D6007a.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The video which is now showed is 1D6006a. So, therefore, I don't know who put it on our screens, but perhaps look at the one you intend to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we can play it a second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't think that you need the beginning of because there was no sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Doctor: Today about 1615 hours a greatly injured patient named Natasa Ucur born in 1985 was brought to the Kasindol hospital. She was injured in Grbavica. During the admission at the surgery ward of the Kasindol hospital we found serious head injuries. The bone structure of the head and brain tissue were damaged. The injuries were lethal and the girl passed away within several minutes. Immediately after this, some five to six minutes later, another ambulance brought in Milica Lalovic born in 1984 who was killed in Grbavica also by a sniper bullet. It wasn't possible to help her, the girl was already dead. Innocent children were being killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, could you tell us who carried out the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you wait until the translation has been finished. It has been by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat: Who carried out the on-site investigations at the place where these two little girls were lethally wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters have not caught your answer. Could you repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The on-site investigation was carried out by members of the crime prevention police of the public security station of Sprsko Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you establish on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Death was established for these two little girls. Also the place from which the sniper bullet had come, the one that killed these two girls, so it was clear that it had come from the positions where members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were. The distance from these positions to this place is also about 200 metres which means that with the naked eye the person who was firing could see that these were children. These two little girls were playing in front of their home, and they were hit by fire from the other side. The fire came from a fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, now all what we have seen and all questions you asked were not focussed on what you say you want to establish. It was mainly focussed on something which was not dispute. That people were shot at from the ABiH side, that victims were killed. That's all not in dispute. You said it's the buildings which we had to attack. I've not heard a word about from what buildings. I've not -- do not know what the date of the incident was. I have not yet, which, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you also have the report of the on-site investigation? That would certainly greatly assist. Then you suddenly get condensed a lot of information including source of fire, perhaps. Instead of hearing after more than 20 years from a witness that the fire came from the other side 200 metres away, which really does not assist us greatly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you established where the firing had come from. Can you tell us from where?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska established that fire came from the direction of the faculty of mechanical engineering. About ten years earlier on, we sent an official report to the Prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, team of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska headed by myself investigated the case once again, and we submitted a report not only for this incident but also for many, many other incidents, sniping, shelling. And this report was filed in terms of direct responsibility of the perpetrators and command responsibility as well. The commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is responsible, and other persons were responsible. And by filing this report, we clearly indicated all the positions from which the victims had been hit and it is precisely all of these positions that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, you apparently are more or less responding to some questions I put to the Defence. You're not answering the question at this moment. If there's any material, we expect the Defence to present that if they want to have this line of questions put. You don't have to elaborate on all that. Mr. Lukic will take care of it. The only thing is usually if incidents are considered to be relevant and important that this Chamber often is provided with the reports of the on-site investigations which we have not seen for the one which is now apparently the subject of examination. Mr. Lukic, would you please keep control over your witness. That's one. And, second, when I earlier said four minutes, it may have been six, but you went far beyond that so try to come with concrete materials on matters which are in dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us briefly do you remember the year when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this occurred in 1995. I think it was the month of March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the reaction of the Army of Republika Srpska was to this incident?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, absolutely, this was not within my domain to think about that at that moment, what the reaction of the Army of Republika Srpska would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move onto a different topic now. Can you tell us what your occupation is today?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already ten years within the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, I investigate war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, I'm in charge of investigations of war crimes against Serbian people. That's one of my priority tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you investigate? Which location.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigations carried out by the team of the Ministry of Interior that I head were into the killings of Serbs in the city of Sarajevo, in Srebrenica, crimes perpetrated by the Mujahed and by the 5th Corps, the Dretelj camp, Konjic. Those were the major cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will dwell a little on Sarajevo. Can you tell us how many camps there were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the research that we carried out, there were 126 camps or places where civilians were held unlawfully in Sarajevo. Which means that there was absolutely no basis for their detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Had I been notified that this witness would give any evidence relating to detention facilities or camps, I would have prepared accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 65 ter summary, Mr. Lukic, could you tell us exactly where you indicated that camps would be part of your -- and I don't have it here with me but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I can even assist because I do have it but because I have a marked up copy, I'll just indicate what there is relating to camps in the 65 ter summary. It says: "The witness also has information about the setting up of prisoner camps for Serbs in Sarajevo such as Viktor Bubanj barracks and the cental prison." That's two, Your Honours, a far cry from 126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that in itself to say that the witness had knowledge about more camps and even a number that's not in itself necessarily outside the scope of the 65 ter, but would you please then focus on what you announced would be the subject of examination in terms of camps, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who gave you orders to investigate war crimes against Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, the minister and the director of police ordered the establishment of a team to investigate war crimes, and when that team was established, we established co-operation with the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina and district prosecutor's offices, and we investigated cases according to instructions we received from prosecutor's offices, and we also carried out pre-investigation inquiries into all the incidents that we learned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the final result of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we submitted to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina and prosecutor's offices of the district over 50 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the number. Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you repeat the number. You said you submitted to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina and prosecutor's offices of the district over ... how many reports or cases or files? How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the city of Sarajevo, over 280 official reports or criminal complaints. I'm talking only about Sarajevo. Only the crimes perpetrated in Sarajevo. In these reports, we established that there were 3.300 victims, civilian victims, on the territory of ten Sarajevo municipalities. Urban municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to call document 1D5095. [In English] My fault. This is the 1D05495. That's the correct -- that is the correct 65 ter number. Sorry, page 3 on B/C/S and English ...

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, can you tell us what kind of list is this.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list that was made based on case files of Serbs killed in Sarajevo and they are in the archive of the MUP in Sarajevo. The MUP of Republika Srpska. This contains the names and years of birth of Serbs killed in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Often for the Prosecution, it's considered better not to broadcast names in such documents and public documents. I haven't heard anything about it, so we let you go. But if you would have similar concerns, then, of course, you could ask for it to be -- not to be broadcast, and if you are seeking admission later to have it under seal. I leave it in your hands. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't have a problem with this document being released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you use as a source of information for this list?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the Court, I would like to explain how we came to establish case files, not this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: You may go on.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the commission was established by the international community, and it was established by the council of ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the parliamentary Assembly. That commission was supposed to investigate the killing of Serb, Croats, Bosniaks and Jews and others on the territory of ten Sarajevo municipalities. Then a MUP team of Republika Srpska joined this commission. We worked following a principle that for every person killed, an individual case file would be opened, and in addition to the name, date of birth, and father's name, it was required to accompany every name with a JM -- with a unique identification number which existed for every citizen of Yugoslavia. Also the birth certificate, the death certificate, and then in every case file, we included copies of all the relevant evidence and indicators that the given person was killed and in which way. So that means the on-site investigation, if any, the photo documentation, video footage, if any, statements of surviving witnesses, statements from family, and all the other evidence that indicated that a crime was perpetrated and also the official report describing the given incident that had been submitted to the prosecutor's office. All this was done not only in writing but also in electronic form. Experts of the Ministry of Interior developed software, so when you type in the name and surname of the victim, you would get the registration number for that victim and if you only have a new report and you don't have that name in the register, then the programme automatically assigned a number to the case. All these case files are still with us. We still have them. And the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal has reviewed them. And when we showed them how we did this work in Sarajevo, they congratulated us, and we still believe today that it was the only way to establish the actual number of civilian victims, not only in the territory of the ten Sarajevo municipalities, but also in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because, in this way, every possibility for manipulation is eliminated. Every citizen had their unique identification number and birth certificate and their families had received death certificates in order to exercise their rights and receive benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "all civilians," which civilians do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "all civilian," I mean civilians of all ethnicities who were killed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosniaks, Serbs, Croats, Jews, all the other citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you use as a source of information about missing persons in this list?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of missing persons, we used, first of all, reports to the ICRC and international organisations dealing with missing persons, reports from families looking for their near and dear. We used, as I said, all court material that was available, all court papers that were written during the investigation, photo documentation, video footage, records of exhumations, crime-scene reports, all the indicators that a given person is, indeed -- was, indeed, a victim of the war, a civilian victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's all -- if I understand you well, this list is exclusively about civilians. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the list contains the names of civilians only. We did not investigate cases of deaths of combatants of Republika Srpska. We only dealt with civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I have difficulties to understand is that this list as is shown to us, a lot of information which you would expect to be available is just not on that list, such as, sometimes, even the year of birth for many, many victims are not available. And do you have any explanation as to the -- how this information which must be available, why it's not on that list? For example, we could look at -- just for an example, could we look at the last page. That's page 214 of this list. Could we have a look at the last page. Could it be enlarged slightly. For both version, the last page. And perhaps for the B/C/S, the semi-last page. One page back. For example, if we look at entry 3022 -- could we enlarge. There, we see the name of that person, his father's name, his first name. Year of birth is not there. Although it's known that it was a doctor, that he was killed by a sniper on the 17th of June, and then all kind of details about that. Why do we not know in what year that doctor was born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This list is not final. These case files are not final. They have not been finalized. All this information was taken from the archives that were accessible to us when we created these case files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If -- if you -- excuse me. Identification numbers and the files containing ID papers where they ae contained were in the territory controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These persons, because they had been killed, were not included in the joint common programme which allows us today to get the name of a particular person with one click. That was a problem. And it's obvious that we still continue working to complete these files and to collect other evidence and relevant indicators pertaining to these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But only on this page for nine persons even the year of birth is not known and if you say it doesn't automatically come in well, if you say it's after close to 20 years that this is the level which we reached, then we can continue. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic, and I'm saying "please proceed," you know you're now approximately one hour over your time and some of your evidence was not about matters in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you've already put my last question, and since the witness provided an explanation in terms of that, I have no questions left for this witness for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I would just like to thank Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for these three exhibits, the video material 1D6006c and 1D6007a, and 1D045 [sic], I would like to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar could you assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 1D06006c receives exhibit number D1214. 65 ter number 1D6007A receives exhibit number D1215. Document number 1D05495 receives exhibit number D1216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. All three admitted into evidence under the numbers mentioned. Ms. Edgerton, are you ready to start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm just looking at the time. I will have about seven minutes before the first break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would prefer to, for the flow of your questions, to take the break now, then we'd consider that. But you could start.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just begin, if I may and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. You find her to your right and Ms. Edgerton is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tusevljak. You can understand everything I say, can you? Can you understand me in your own language, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my language, yes, I'm receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to stay with this list for a while, with your list, and ask you some questions on it. Now, you've indicated in your testimony a few moments ago that this list relates to a project to establish the victims of the war, and you referred to civilians of all ethnicities who were killed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosniak, Serbs, Croats, Jews, all the victims of war. Now I've had a look at this list and all the names on the list, and but for two Ukrainians, I've only seen Serb names on this list. This is a list of people who have a Serb surname; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because my task was to establish precisely the victimisation of Serbs. Others had other tasks. Within that commission, my task was to see how many Serbs fell victim. That was my task. My task was not to establish something else. It's a question of an assignment, a task, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that mean that your answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my task was to investigate cases when Serbs fell victim. It's 2007, 2008 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've also testified this morning that this list was based on case files of Serbs killed in Sarajevo. Now, there's a large number of people on this list who were victimised in locations outside Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's not a single victim there that fell victim outside the territory of the ten municipalities of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at this list as we can and go to number 92. And I'm sorry, I don't have the page numbers immediately for these entries. So just look at number -- entry number 91 and 92 and for that matter, have a look at number 94 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're on e-court page 10, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There are three names of victims who were victimised in Kladanj. Kladanj isn't in Sarajevo, is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these are probably persons --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question. Kladanj isn't in Sarajevo, is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kladanj is not in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have, in addition to this, at numbers 229, 707, 842, and 1462 entries related to victims in Olovo. Olovo isn't in Sarajevo either, is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that here. What's the number that you said? I haven't got it here on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question is: Olovo isn't in Sarajevo, is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Olovo is not in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The list contains nine entries for people who were victimised in Konjic. 11 entries for people who were victimised in Kijevo. One from Rogatica. One from Sjemec and ten entries for people who were victimised in Kiseljak. None of those places are anywhere in any one of the ten pre-war Sarajevo municipalities, are they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kijevo is within the area of the municipality of Trnovo. Kiseljak is a border area. Well, we published this list, we made it public. It's on the Internet. At the very end of this list, we said that this is a preliminary list, that it is not final, that all citizens who see any omission - and this was a huge undertaking - they can intervene. Sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I stop you there. That's not the issue. The issue is not whether matters should be corrected. The issue is that you say that these are -- is a list of those who fell victim in the ten municipalities of Sarajevo. Ms. Edgerton is telling that you on this list, that there is a considerable number of people who were reported not to have died. So whether there are any mistakes and whether these civilians could comment, that's another matter, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a huge number of mistakes, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry -- please. There's 3.300 names of victims here, not these 30 or 40. Well, I don't have all the files here because in the file that exists for each and every one of these victims, you would be able to see other evidence that indicates why they are here. I cannot see it on the basis of this list, but I can see it in the file. Somebody just compiled this list on the basis of files. It's not I or a member of my team that did this. Somebody else leafed through this and made this table. We did not work on that. We worked on the files, on the basis of which this table was made. So all of these questions that the Prosecutor has put can be determined only if we go to the actual files of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that apparently the information as we have it in the list is not reliable for making any findings, because the explanation why it is different from what it looks like on this list is not to be found in this list itself. I leave it that to that for the time being and we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, just before the break and before we break, and it's my mistake, it was also reminded to me by Mr. Tieger, I had actually intended, Your Honour, and I wasn't fast enough on the uptake and listening to my memories, I had intended to ask for this list we're discussing now to be marked for identification pending cross-examination and I'd just like to put that on the record now and ask Your Honours if we may reconsider, and it's 1D1216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you wanted to have it marked for identification pending cross-examination. Well, -- we have admitted it already so you could ask to reconsider that decision and perhaps do it after the cross-examination or after this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, although I did use the word "reconsider," I would like Your Honours to reconsider the admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now or after --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... after the end of the cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the end of the cross-examination. We will do that. It certainly be helpful if you remind us to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, of course, my apologies for not noticing the numbers as I was going along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, apologies accepted. We will take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. Mr. Tusevljak, you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I briefly deal with one procedural matter, which is about D745. On the 26th of August of this year, the Prosecution stated in court that it does not oppose the admission of D745. Since an earlier objection of the Prosecution was the reason that D745 was marked for identification, the Chamber now admits D745 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I'd like to stay with this list for a while, actually. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is D1216.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: D1216, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- 1216. I mispronounced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we're talking about mispronunciation I misspoke about Beara before the break when I refer to the list that people had not died where I should have added in Sarajevo. That was a mistake and it could create some confusion that's the reason why I'm trying to correct it now immediately on the record. Please proceed, and, again, apologies for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This list that's the same list you spoke about when you testified here in the Dragomir Milosevic and the Stanisic and Zupljanin prosecutions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just parts of the list because probably this list has been extended, I think. Because investigations are ongoing. I've already told you that it's not final. It's a preliminary list. It is being supplemented to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Now, then, let's see if we can have a look at 65 ter number 32976. Now I'm just going to show you the first page for a second. This is the cover page of a book provided by a Defence witness for Dr. Karadzic, and his name as you can see was Dusan Zurovac. And this book was prepared or published in 2006. And if you look at the bottom of the cover page, it even says: "Prepared by Dusan Zurovac." Now if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I object. Because Mr. Tusevljak testified about a list of missing and killed persons that were the result of a MUP investigation and here we have a private individual who wrote a book and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know yet what the question is. So let's wait for that. And as soon as you stand, Mr. Lukic, I usually understand that as a request to interfere, and perhaps you were a bit too early on your feet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I'm going to have us turn to Sanction actually because, Mr. Tusevljak, I'd like to have us look at the first page of your list side by side with the first page of this book. And Ms. Stewart has that available for us. If you'd just give us a couple of minutes. So what you should see beside you is the first page of your -- or page -- this is -- have a look at entry number 3, actually, in your list, which is on the left-hand side, beside and it's an entry for somebody by the name of Risto Avram and then go over and look at the same entry for Risto Avram with the same date of birth, same father's name and same event details. That's at page 2 in Mr. Zurovac's book. The two entries are word for word identical, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, shall we be able to see the lists in English at some stage. They're both in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I was doing that for the witness's ease and I'm wondering if I could invite Your Honours to look at the English version of D1216 on your own e-court so that you're able to follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The important thing is to compare the two lists so that's why I'm asking at some stage you'll give the same lists both on the same page but in English for us to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what is in Sanction, of course, we could not get on our on screens. So, therefore, if you say compare the English then at least for what is presented in Sanction we are unable to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could make my point with the witness and then we will go to the English pages in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you see those two entries are word for word identical; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now again, we are looking at the list presented by the witness entry number 3 and on the right side of the screen, it is -- it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Entry number 6 [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's actually the entry at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then there it appears that's for let me see, 3 seems to be -- yes. 3 corresponds with Avram and I see Risto and I see 1952, and I see a rather long description in which at least the date, 25th of 6th of 1992, appears in both the lists. Is that what you are --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we are with you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They're identical, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for this at the end where we say that he was exhumed according to the information of the central records for searching for missing persons. I've already said to you when I was answering the questions put by the Defence that the first preliminary list of 2.500 names --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to answer. I would like to clarify something if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it is Ms. Edgerton who puts the questions to you and if she thinks you're moving away too much from her question then whatever you wish to explain, if it's relevant you'll given an opportunity to later in re-examination. But if she interrupts you in fairness, of course, then you'd have to follow her. And I'm a bit lost where the exhumation is mentioned in the last lines because at least what I see is that there is some similarity there as well, the word exhumation at the semi-last line, a date is there. But I leave it your hands, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's see how far Ms. Edgerton comes and then your help is appreciated, I take it, later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I just want to say with these two pages and what we'll be able to since we're staying with the two pages is go over to the English language page for Their Honours. Have a look at your list at entries number 4, 5, 6, even number 9, and they're almost identical with the entries in the book by Dusan Zurovac, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could now go over to the English version of D1216, just the first page, so Their Honours so see the entries we've been referring to. D1216. Page 3 it is of D1216 actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's still the B/C/S. Yes, now we need English for both lists: The book and the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, because of time constraints we don't have an English translation of the first page of that book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. But the page where we see the entries which you wanted to compare.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can give you the B/C/S -- the B/C/S entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no English translation for the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Our translators have been working at great speed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But then, of course, being unable to compare the entry as if it is about exhumations and the differences where we cannot verify it ourselves, Mr. Lukic, if your offer to assist still stands, I would appreciate.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to assist regarding the difference in explanation in the previous document shown from Mr. Zurovac's book. I doubt that I can assist with this in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Because I think that the witness said something about that information was added in your list and we see there the last portion of the text being exhumed at the Aerodromsko Naselje settlement and identified on the 10th of -- it looks January, I think, 2000, data of the office for tracing missing persons. What's the difference between the two --

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. The difference is that in the list, D1216, it reads in the last sentence: "Information of the information for searches for the missing persons," and in Zurovac's book it says he was exhumed in the Aerodrom neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which appears that the fact of the exhumation in the Aerodrom neighbourhood is in all [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's in both.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But now you having seen, Mr. Tusevljak, that the entries on the first page are almost identical I want to tell that you we've actually gone through the book we've had a speaker of your language go through that book and see that most of the entries are identical. So I'd like to ask you what you spoke to -- in relation to what you spoke to in your testimony in-chief here, whose list is it? Is it your list or is it Mr. Zurovac's list which was published in 2005?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the list of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, not the list of Mr. Zurovac. This last word, "information from the office for searches for the missing" means that the MUP of Republika Srpska, concerning the killing of Avram Nedjo Risto, received information from the office for searches for the missing of Republika Srpska and it's obvious that the same information was received by Mr. Zurovac from the same office. That's why I said it was important to stress that this is information obtained from the office for searches for the missing that Mr. Zurovac obtained too. And it's probable that the information we got from that office - and obviously Mr. Zurovac got it as well - may coincide because the same information was received by the MUP and Mr. Zurovac when he was collecting material for this book.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Can I just ask a question for clarification. I thought you said earlier that this list that you were talking about from your office was compiled based on the information from the investigation files, not from the office of tracing missing persons. Am I -- did I misunderstand you? You actually said you didn't compile this but you -- but the people who compiled the list did so getting their information from the files, individual files for investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should clarify. Information concerning persons who were victimised was obtained from police sources, from military sources, from the centre for investigating war crimes in Belgrade, the office for tracing missing persons, the records of the ICRC. All these archives were reviewed by us and everything pertaining to certain persons was included in the case files for these people. This list is just an excerpt from these case files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you for the explanation. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, did you check this list? Have you had a look at it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this one here? I did not check it, but it was made by operative officers of the MUP of Republika Srpska who used archives and case filings that are in my office to create this list. So each person included in this list should have a case file in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what happens when you have an entry that appears to be a duplicate?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that we have software in our computer set up in such a way that when we have the same name and surname and even the same father's name, the case file is pulled up and if we find out that it's the same person we put additional documentation in that case file and if we establish that it's a different person we open a new case file.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So let's go back to D1216 and go over to a couple of entries that I have some questions about then. I've -- first of all, want to go to number 2749 on the list. It's at B/C/S page 224 and English page 199. And you see the name I'm interested in at the top of the page in your language, 2749, that's Olga Cokic. Now, Mr. Tusevljak, if you go over to entry number 2832, it's on B/C/S page 230 and English page 204. And, for the record, she's at the bottom in English, page 199. So we're going to entry 2832. You see that the very same -- a woman by the very same name with the identical father's name and the identical year of birth is listed. And frankly, they have the descriptions of the way in which they went missing is very, very similar. The woman at entry number 2749 went missing in Sarajevo on 18 May 1992 and the same woman in entry 2832 was killed by a sniper on 18 May 1992. That's a potential duplicate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to object because it was said incorrectly that these were identical persons. There is a difference in surname. The person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel has said these numbers too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you want to object on that basis you should do it in such a way that it doesn't give guidance to the witness, such as misrepresents the evidence or misrepresented or could I invite to read exactly the names on both lists and otherwise you have an opportunity to address the matter in re-examination. But the way in which do it, Mr. Lukic, is not the way it should be done. At the same time, Ms. Edgerton has now heard what you said and certainly will think about it and when continuing her cross-examination. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll go onto another entry. Perhaps we can could go over to English and B/C/S page 76. Have a look at entries number 897 and 903, Mr. Tusevljak. They both relate to a woman by the name of Sofia Eric and while number 897 has actually no year of birth or father's name, they both relate to women who were exhumed from the Lav cemetery on 27 August 2000. That's another potential duplicate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without looking into the case files, I cannot know whether it's a duplicate or not. The only criterion is the case file and the information contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why Ms. Edgerton phrased her question about a potential duplicate. The question is whether you see anything here which would make you conclude that there's no need to go back to the original files and that, on the basis of what is found on this list, you could already exclude a duplicate, because if not it is a potential duplicate. Any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this 897, we don't have the father' name. We have the father's name for 903. But some things coincide. We don't have the date of disappearance up there. It means it's 1993. And since this is documentation we received from the office for tracing missing persons, it's probable that this office has records for two persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was not the issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We're just going to one more, both on the same page in English and B/C/S, page 99, and it's entries 1199 and 1200. Now, they both relate to a man by the name of Zdravko Karakas who was born in 1952. Same date of birth. Do you see -- and same father's name. Do you see a potential duplicate in that entry?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this concerns two different sources of information. In the first one, as you can see, the person went missing in Sarajevo in 1992; and in the second, it says he was killed by a shell on 22nd June 1992. So, according to the information we received, or the documentation that was available to us, we were not in a position at that time to establish whether it is the same person or not because the information on the manner of killing differs. One is that he was taken to Kasin and killed and the other was from Oslobodjenje, 18 January 1992, where it says that this person was killed by a shell. That's the difference and that's why these names which are the same are on the same list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If may just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you said it was reported he was taken to, et cetera, that's -- were you reading from 1198 instead of from 1199? Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, sorry, it's my mistake. It says here he went missing in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the data was received from his aunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just wanted to point that you were reading from the -- another record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So on the basis of an identical surname, an identical father's name, and an identical date of birth, as well as an identical first name, do you see a potential duplicate in that entry, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Identical year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, to be precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said this was a preliminary list and until we check the case files to see what might indicate differently we cannot know looking at this list. In Bosnia-Herzegovina to this day, when you type in the names and the father's name you often get hundreds of names.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, earlier another list was presented which was published in 2005 and Ms. Edgerton, although we had no opportunity yet to verify that, said that the entries were -- most of the cases exactly the same. Now if would that would be true for what is found in 2005, do I understand that finding duplicates since 2005, that is, over the last ten years has not reached a level where with such similar family name, first name, father's name, year of birth, approximate time when disappeared or killed that you had no opportunity yet to verify on the basis of the underlying documentation whether it is really a duplicate or whether it still is a potential duplicate only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These could only be potential duplicates not real duplicates. Investigation continues and things change. We had a lot more information in the early days that we found out is incorrect after doing some work and we eliminated such persons. We didn't include them. We have a lot of dubious case files still where we are unable to determine the validity of the evidence, and we didn't include them at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... one second. This is all general considerations. Are you able to tell us exactly what was done with Mr. Karakas Dusan in 1199 and 1200. Could you give us details on verification which would either tell you that they were two different persons or that it is, indeed, a duplicate? If you know tell us; if you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I cannot know because we have 3.300 names. I cannot memorize each of then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not blaming you for it. But I just want to know whether you can answer that question. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at 65 ter number 33024.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, I want to ask you: Would you agree with me, Mr. Tusevljak, that duplicates, potential duplicates on any list, would tend to elevate the numbers of people listed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We never had that intention.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, it's -- I'm not asking about your intention. I'm asking if for whatever reason there's two people, two names on the list which have an identical surname, an identical first name, an identical father's name and an identical year of birth when only one after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to object because it's impossible to establish the identicalness of one person only on the basis of information or data cited by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're answering the question rather than to object against the question. Now, Ms. Edgerton, your question originally was that if you have duplicates on a list that that tends to elevate the number of people listed. Of course, if a person, the same person appears twice then that adds one to the list. I mean, what's there for a witness to add anything which not everyone would consider to be obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. He did say no, though, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard his answer on a question which -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, the list you see in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way in all fairness the witness said no on the basis of a wrong understanding of the question. Because he said, No, we had no intention. So apparently he understood your question wrongly, the question was not needed to be put at all and we'll now continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, in front of you, you see a list that's drawn from the names that appeared in the larger list we've been talking about. And we've been able to identify over 60 potential duplicate names. So, Mr. Tusevljak, it looks like your offices haven't screened the list for potential duplicates, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list was screened and filtered many times, and if you take away even these -- this number of duplicates, still you remain with over 3.000 people killed. There is a small percentage of errors that can appear anywhere but it's negligible compared to the number of victims shown in this list based on the existing case files. Why do I want to tell that you it's not our intention to manipulate? This list was put up on the Internet and everyone can react. That's one. Second, it was made for the joint commission where the representatives for Serbs on that commission were supposed to prove for each name of this list, that it was a civilian victim. It had to be presented to the Bosniak and the Croat and every other side. And that other side had the possibility to react, like you are reacting now, to anything wrong with any of the names, to prevent any manipulation. So it was not our intention to maximise the number of victims but to get evidence that would enable us to establish the actual number of victims. This was not driven by politics. This was a police investigation. Of course, there is always the possibility of human error, but it's negligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're giving a long answer on an allegation that was never made. The simple question was that you haven't screened it for duplicates. That's the only simple factual question. Did your office find time or have an opportunity to deal with those potential duplicates or have they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- wherever we established there was, indeed, a duplicate, we eliminated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And have not, for those here listed here, 30 names which appear approximately the same twice, you did not have an opportunity yet to verify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask Ms. Edgerton, who prepared this list we have on the screen in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This list was prepared internally within the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means at the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to put on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you also agree that what you consider to be potential duplicates at least there is some difference in spelling very often. So therefore, what the potential of those potential duplicates is still to be seen because there are noticeable differences as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now today in your testimony, you also told His Honour -- Their Honours that the list, D1216 is a list of civilians only. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you know there are some soldiers on your list.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be members of the Army of Republika Srpska but, at the moment of death, they were not militarily engaged. They were not on the front line, they were away from the front line, they were wearing civilian clothes, et cetera. There is no one here who died on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- actually, let's have a look at the list again. Let's go over to entry number 1563. It's English and B/C/S page 129.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we need the long list, isn't it, not the potential duplicates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can ask the question without waiting for the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You would also, since you were able to answer that question to a certain extent affirmatively, although with a comment about the status, at the moment these people were killed, you would also be able to confirm that your list includes members of the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are commenting on -- you are -- you're giving testimony. You shouldn't do that. I mean, if there's anything to be dealt with, you do it later in re-examination. And we do not know yet the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So please be aware that this fully inappropriate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now that we've got the list in front of us, have a look at entry number 1563. That's Radenko Magazin. He was killed on Dobrovoljacka Street. He's a member of the JNA; right. You put his rank there. He's a soldier; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's the victim of a war crime. We are talking about victims of war crimes here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness, you talked about civilians. You said they were all civilians. You didn't say they were victims of war crimes. You said they were civilians. And I would invite you to make a clear distinction between the two. Please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I do apologise. On this list, there are victims of war crimes. And since soldiers are also victims of war crimes, that is to say, they were not killed in combat, they are also contained in this list. I'm sorry I didn't explain it the first time. So these are victims of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How many soldiers are on this list?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not make that kind of distinction. But it's very clear here. It's always mentioned here if somebody is a soldier. That means that that person was killed as part of a war crime in Dobrovoljacka, in a camp in Sarajevo, so it's all mentioned here in the notes. But such a person was not killed as a result of his activities as a member of the army. Rather, he fell victim to a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is you've never taken this computer-generated list over to your own Ministry of Defence and run it through their systems to identify how many VRS soldiers are on the list; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we worked in the Ministry of Interior, and I already told you in which way we did our work. It was based on how a person fell victim. That is how we compiled this list. At that moment, it didn't matter whether that person was a member of the VRS or the JNA. That person was a victim of a war crime, which means that that is against international law so that person is a war crimes victim.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know either that you have members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on this list, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are also members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, those who fell victim to war crimes and that's the situation in Kazani where members of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade precisely killed Serbs who were within their own ranks. And I also a have a series of examples. I know it by heart because this is it a case that we submitted to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and they are victims of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I didn't ask you about Kazani. My colleague can do that in re-examination if you want to talk about it. The question was simple: Do you know or don't you that you have members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on this list.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've just given you an answer, that there are members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who are Serbs and victims of war crimes and they were killed by the same members of that army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So how many members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina do you have on this list then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you the same answer that I gave for members of the Army of Republika Srpska and who were victims of war crimes we did not establish that. We did not make a distinction there and that was not the aim of this investigation. Their affiliations of any kind. Their affiliations with an ethnic group, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you insisted that this list was only civilians earlier today, and you insisted that actually when you talked about this list and in the Dragomir Milosevic case and in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case when you insisted it was only civilians, that was actually incorrect, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not understanding each other. This has to do with war crimes victims. That is to say, all the persons whose names are on this list were unlawfully killed. So these are persons who were killed. At the moment when they were killed, when they lost their lives, they were not acting in their capacity of military personnel. They were not carrying out combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it - but just a clarifying question - there are quite a number of people on this list as reported missing. Were they victims of war crimes as well, or is that just unknown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously these persons who are recorded here as missing are actually persons who were taken by military or police organs from their apartments and then all trace was lost of them. Obviously because time went by - it's already been 20 years - well, already after a few years, it was clear that they were victims of war crimes because they could not just disappear. They were taken away. They were taken to a camp or somewhere. They were killed along the way or in the camp and their bodies were removed and it is evident that they are victims of war crimes, in terms of the way in which they went missing. You know, they didn't go in an unknown direction from their apartments. They were taken away by organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes the entry just says "missing" or "went missing" and for quite a few others, it says they were taken from their apartment, et cetera. But I do understand from your answer that you are assuming that if there's no further data in here, that you assume that they were taken, that you assume that they were killed because they could not just disappear. That's your reasoning for such conclusions. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And you will see that when speaking of missing persons it usually says that this is information provided by the office for searching for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've not done any checks into these names of missing persons to make sure that they're not still alive, have you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, we checked. That's done every day for every day, from the moment when they were reported as missing. To this day. There are their families, there are witnesses, so it's an illusion. I wish they were all alive. I would be so happy, believe me if you found 1.000 persons or 2.000 persons who were alive after all and that none of them went missing. Rather, that they were all living somewhere abroad. I wish it was that way because I have lots of relatives and friends amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you checked to see what their status was, did you by any chance check and see whether they had registered to vote in 1997 or in 2000? That would be an easy check, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list was compiled in 2007, as were the files, so it's all of 12 years after the end of the war. We did find different cases, somebody reported, say, in 1992, that a person went missing and whenever we found this person to be alive. I didn't need a voters' list. It's enough for me to enter the database of the CIPS because in order to be able to vote every person has to have an ID card. And this information is accessible to all my operatives. It's sufficient to check the new ID or the new passport that everybody has so this would just be additional work that wouldn't really lead us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're here confirming that there's no one on this list who is still alive. Is that what I'm to take from that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of these persons are alive, those who are here. At least on the basis of the checks that we've run so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, could we have look, please, at 65 ter number 32974. So, Mr. Tusevljak, what we did when we received this list, is we looked at this list against the voter registers for the elections in 1997 and 1998 and 2000 and we came up with a list of people who were potentially alive. And we took that list - and there were 80 names - and we pared it down to ten people and we sent that list down to our field office in Sarajevo and here you see the results of what we asked them to do. We forwarded it to our field office who then forwarded it to authorities in Republika Srpska, for the Ministry of Interior, and to authorities in the Federation to see if these people could be located. And I'll show you their responses. Let's just go down a little bit and look at number 1 on this list. His name is Zoran Gajic. And in B/C/S you'll have to go over to page 2, please. Zoran Gajic, who appears at entry number 511 on your list, lives in Brcko district. If we go down to the next name, Dragan Zrnic, who appears at number 949 of your list, he also lives in Brcko district. And if we go over to page 2 in English and just a little bit further down the page in B/C/S. Vitomir Jaric, who is entry number 1080 on your list, lives in Zvornik. And Zoran Krsmanovic, number 1394 on your list, lives in Bijeljina. So there's four actually still alive. And one Lena Njegovanovic, number 1967 on your list, was alive and registered in Trebinje in 2010. And then if we go over to Annex D of this document at B/C/S page ten and English pages 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'll just be a couple of more minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see -- I'll wait until we see the B/C/S. You see that Gajic, Zrnic and Krsmanovic were all personally contacted. Gajic was a soldier and police officer.
