He was never deployed in Sarajevo. And that's what he told the authorities when he was contacted. Zrnic was a former JNA officer absorbed into the VRS and later a member of the police. He wasn't missing at all. And Krsmanovic, and we have to go over to the next page in both languages. Krsmanovic -- pardon me, if we could go back over to page 3 in this document and page 4 in B/C/S. Krsmanovic, whom you allege was taken into June 1992 from his apartment in Novo Sarajevo, was deployed in Bijeljina during the war and never in or around Sarajevo. So, Mr. Tusevljak, my question to you is: The information on your list in terms of the missing is unreliable, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would like to see that list now. Why this persons are on that list. I now have persons here with certain information and then I don't see those notes, why that person is on that list. I'm talking about the list of persons about 3.300, and you are referring to ten. So I'd had to have this huge brain in order to remember 3.300 persons and the reasons why they're on this list. And I really cannot see that now, and I don't know if these are the persons who are on the list because over here it says reason why these persons are on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll look at that, if need be, after the break. Because we'll first take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting, I'd like to briefly deal with D768. On the 24th of August of this year, the Defence advised the Chamber and the Prosecution through an e-mail that the parties are reached an agreement that the handwriting on page 2 column 4 of D768 reads: "Yugoslav." Since in outstanding matter was the reason D768 retained its MFI status, the Chamber now admits D768 into evidence. The Chamber also puts on the record that the Defence in the same e-mail stated that the parties had agreed that the source of this handwriting is unknown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the list overall, you pointed out in your testimony in-chief that you said the list and your files contain the names and the years of birth of the people listed and their father's name. And when His Honour Judge Orie then queried you about a missing -- at transcript page 16 and 17 a missing year of birth for one of your entries, you pointed out the list was not finalised. So in counting up the entries on your list, we realised that a total of 1.437 entries were missing a first name or a father's name or a year of birth. So, similarly, we should consider those entries as inconclusive or not finalized cases. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only those 1.000-something, but none of these are final and complete. This is not a list that was verified by that commission. I already said that this was taken from the files and attachments, evidence, have been included in these files pertaining to the victimisation of these persons. So the list is not final to this day. It's still being worked on. However, it is evident that all these persons that are on the list, that there is some evidence about these persons that indicate what their fate was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, then, when we talk about their fate, you would agree with me that this list includes the names of Serbs in Bosnian-held Sarajevo who were killed as a result of shelling and sniping by VRS forces; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's please go back to the list, D1216, English page 193 and B/C/S page 213. I want to go to entry number 2597. Right. Entry number 2597 is for Jadranka Tendzera and your information, as I understand it -- she was born in 1963, and your information, as I understand, says she was killed by a shell at Vojnicko Polje on 4 February 1994, information from the centre for investigating crimes against the Serb people in Belgrade. Now I want to go to P867 now, please. P867 is the investigative file for a shelling in Dobrinja, which is Bosnian-held Sarajevo, where nine people were killed and 20 were wounded. And could we please go over to page 6 in both languages of this document. And page 6 is the second page of the on-site investigative report. This on-site investigative report lists the victims and you see Jadranka Tendzera is number 1 on the list and in addition to her, there is Enver Mustagrudic, Saida Bakcevic, Ermin Kolar and Aisa Sito and an unidentified child. And then listed below are three additional victims who succumbed to their injuries. So, Mr. Tusevljak, not only is your information wrong, and you were incorrect in the assertion that you just made about Mrs. Tendzera, you've listed the only Serb victim in a large-scale shelling in Bosnian-held Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we see here that we had mentioned that this is information from the centre for the investigation of war crimes in Belgrade. That's very clear. That is to say, we used the information that we had, that is, information from the centre for investigation of war crimes from Belgrade, what we mentioned that, we did not have this document here. I could take a look at it and I could see if it's the same person. If it's Dobrinja or Vojnicko Polje, because they are two completely different neighbourhoods in Sarajevo. Completely different neighbourhoods, separate. One is Dobrinja, the other one is Vojnicko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dobrinja was Bosnian-held and Vojnicko Polje was Serb-held during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. None of the two. Only one part of Dobrinja was under Serb control. The main part of Dobrinja was under BH army control and the same with Vojnicko Polje. One part was controlled by the VRS, the other by ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, if we give you, after the next break, a copy of this investigative report and a copy of Mrs. Tendzera's death certificate, is that going to help you confirm whether or not there are Serb victims of VRS shelling and sniping into Bosnian-held Sarajevo on this list?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that there were casualties killed by the Serb forces, but our intention was to put on the list anyone who was Serb and was killed in Sarajevo by Bosnian forces. Through our investigations, we received reports or found out from witnesses that many people who were victimised in camps or were killed were shown -- were held out to be victims killed by Serbs which was not the case. You have the case of Romeo and Juliet from Sarajevo, where the girl was killed by --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you want to talk about that case, you can do it in your re-direct examination. I'd like to focus on another incident. Let's have a look at P6482, please, and I'm going ask you about a couple of entries on your list now. Gordana Bogdanovic, your entry says she was -- your entry says: Killed civilians on the territory of Sarajevo, information provided by the centre for crimes committed over the Serbian people, Belgrade. She got killed by a shell 5 February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go over, please, to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Go down to number 8 on this list in both languages. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there no problem with broadcasting this list?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll defer to my colleague to my right. Not to be broadcast, he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he'll verify and advise us in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: She appears at number 8 on the list. If we go further down to number 33 on this list, we see Marija Knezevic whose name appears in entry at 1269 on your list. Ruza Malovic who is entry number 1601 on your list appears at number 39 and actually in addition, you know, just in terms of Serb victims, there's an additional three on this list that aren't even referred to on your list; Klacar, Vojnovic - four - Cesic, Cebrez [phoen]. So in addition to victims of the incident for which General Galic has been convicted and sentences, your list includes victims of the market-place massacre in February 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to let me see my list again to see the explanation why these people were included. Because I don't know by heart. I have to see the explanation next to the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back to your list for a second because it might be somewhat illuminating in terms of the level of information that you provide about these individuals. Let's go to number 1601 on D1216. It's at ET in B/C/S, page 132. We see the entry for Ruza Malovic in front of us in your language. And now in English. The data on Mrs. Malovic simply says, Killed civilian in Sarajevo. It doesn't provide an indication as to whether or not it happened in Bosnian-held Sarajevo or Serb-held Sarajevo. It doesn't provide an indication as to the date of the incident. This kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 5th February [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5th February.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Markale was in 1994, February. If I remember well. The 1st of February; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we heard quite a bit of evidence that it was on the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this kind of deficient data risks being misleading as to where an incident might have happened, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I'm telling you, the list is preliminary and the investigation continues. What you saying now, all of this is at the stage of checks and adding to the material. This is not a shut book. It's an open book. It's open to all people of goodwill to provide evidence on killing of Serbs in Sarajevo. We have never tried to run away from any kind of correction from day one because our purpose was to get to the truth. So that those who are responsible for crimes be held accountable, be brought to justice. There are investigations ongoing, both in the cantonal prosecutor's office and the district prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you haven't updated this list since the verdict was rendered in the Prosecution of General Galic, have you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now different policemen are working on investigations of war crimes for the city of Sarajevo. I am in engaged in other work, and I have had no insight in a long time what corrections have been made.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like that ask the

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. But I think where the case files are in the Security Services Centre in eastern Sarajevo there is a Department for Investigating War Crimes and that department has the possibility, every time they obtain new evidence, to include that evidence in the case file of the relevant victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you don't know when it was updated the last time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So just based on two incidents we've been discussing now, shelling in Dobrinja and the market-place shelling the next day, it looks like the only narrow thing we can be sure of in terms of this list is that it does -- are you not hearing translation, interpretation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's just that I absolutely don't agree with you, and that's why I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you first listen to the question before you start expressing agreement or disagreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The only thing we can be sure of on this list in terms of up-to-date investigation is that it includes Serb victims of shelling and sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The way you are putting the question, it's impossible to answer it with a yes or no. If I understood the question correctly, and I hope I did, you are trying with this list of 3.300 names and case files is to reduce it to two incidents and there are 3.300 incidents involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not expected to comment of what the intentions of Ms. Edgerton are. That's not something for a witness. The question was simply whether it's true or not that Serb victims of shelling and sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo were included. Ms. Edgerton, I take it that you did not want to say whether all of those were included but at least some of cases of Serb victims of shelling and sniping are included on this list, whether you would agree with that. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put the next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If investigations into this list have been ongoing, you would have seen, wouldn't you, that there are records of contemporaneous investigations that point to where it's been concluded that people on this list have been victims of Serb shelling. I'll give you another example. Let's go to number 1316; English and B/C/S page 109. Your entry for Vera Kovackovic says she was killed on 30 August 1993 by an artillery shell in Sarajevo. Information from the centre for investigating war crimes -- pardon me, investigating crimes against the Serbian people in Belgrade. Now, first of all, where we see an entry at that says "Sarajevo," are we meant to infer Bosnian-held Sarajevo or Serb-held Sarajevo? What kind of location -- what kind of precision are we meant to draw from that kind of designation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As can you see in each of these cases, it says this is information from the centre for investigating crimes against Serb people in Belgrade. That's what they had at that time. As you were able to see, in some cases we have information from the office for tracing missing persons. We have information from the black book by Toholj and we have witness testimony as well. We always put in the nota bene where the information came from and that's why I'm telling you, the investigations are ongoing. They continue. Now, are they quick enough? I, myself, am not satisfied. I'm unhappy that we don't have more evidence included in the files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I interrupt you because I'd like to hear an answer to the question. If, in this column, it says "Sarajevo," how do you interpret that even if it comes from Belgrade sources? Do you interpret this as Sarajevo Bosnian-held or Serb-held or both, or ... what's your understanding of a reference to Sarajevo in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you've answered the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where it says absolutely nothing about the place of the incident, are we similarly meant to infer that it is within Bosnian-held Sarajevo or Serb-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, okay, there are a couple of cases here such as Goran Kovackovic killed by a shell, information from the centre for investigating crimes against Serb people in Belgrade, which means this contains only information that was available at that time in 1996 or 1997 when these case files were compiled and when this list was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the answer is, it could be either one; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it could be both.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'd like to leave the list for a while and move on to an area that you were discussing in your evidence in-chief the very first day you came here, and it was about Muslim arming before the war. You talked about a shipment of 400 sniper rifles at transcript page 37070 to 37073, and that you said was an event that happened in 1991. And then you talked about a document, D1108, that was issued by the chef de cabinet of Delimustafic, ordering the relocation of weapons and ammunition from Rakovica to Zlatiste. Now, I just want to ask you a little bit about Rakovica. You said Rakovica was guarded by the SJB of Ilidza. It's correct, isn't it, that the forces of the Ilidza SJB were mainly Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The chief of the police station was my colleague Edin Milic and the ethnic structure was balanced. The chief of the police station was Bosniak. I'm not talking about the heads of department for crime prevention or other departments --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's fine. You answered my question with a no. The police commander was Tomo Kovac; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that's a lower portion than the chief of police station, considerably lower.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in July 1995, Tomo Kovac was the deputy minister of the interior for the Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now you said also that you knew about the security situation in the area of Rakovica at the time this was alleged to have happened, 1991. And you knew that the area of Rakovica was ethnically mixed. Now you would also know that by the end of May 1992 Rakovica, the whole area of Rakovica had been taken over by Serb forces; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the July 1992 and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there's a huge difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm asking you, since you knew so much about the security situation in the area of Rakovica at the date of this document which was July 1991, you would know that by the end of May 1992 the whole area of Rakovica had been taken by Serb forces. You knew that; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the security situation from July 1991 when the security was guaranteed to everyone. We had a joint police force and all other joint things. There was no security risk in Rakovica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question at all. Did you know that by the end of May 1992 Serb forces took the area of Rakovica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that Serb forces took it. We lived there. We couldn't occupy something where we lived. It was ours. How would we take it over? How could Serb forces take it over? We lived there, we were attacked. We were not the ones who were attacked. How could we occupy our own places? My family has lived in Sarajevo for 150 years, now there's no one. Thousands of my relatives had to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, listen carefully to the question Ms. Edgerton will now put to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back to time a little bit to March 1992. You're a member of the police and a very senior member of the police so would you have known that under Kovac's command in March 1992, the Serb police blocked the MUP warehouse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud. Mr. Mladic is -- no audible volume. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- blocked the MUP warehouse at Dugi Potok and [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, don't interrupt Ms. Edgerton when she is phrasing a question. You have an opportunity to answer to it but first you have to listen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- and distributed arms to the Serbs. I'm simply asking because you were clearly a senior member of the police at the time you were familiar by your own admission with what was going on in the area of Ilidza in 1991, I'm asking you if you knew about these events in March and in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1992, there were no events at all except that the first and the second barricades happened, where a member of a Serb wedding party was killed. After that, in March, there were no more events. And on 4 April, the war began in the territory of Sarajevo and that warehouse was in the territory under the control of the MUP and the Army of Republika Srpska. There was no need to block anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I want to go to Zlatiste that you also talked about. Now in discussing that document, you said, you describe Zlatiste and you said it used to be a hotel, restaurant on top with warehouses below. But my question to you is this. Apart from what you read in that document, D1108, you actually had no personal knowledge that ammunition and weapons from Rakovica might have been located to Zlatiste, did you? It was only based on what you read in the document.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I said that based on documents. I spoke primarily about 400 sniper rifles that went to Citluk, the Islamic religious community drove it away in their van and I personally was involved. And the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska found these documents in Rakovica facility where it was obvious how much was shipped away and already then in that year, I knew how much was shipped away from which facility. That was a secret in July 1991 so how could I know it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now irrespective of whatever might have happened in July 1991 and whatever weapons may or may not have been moved, you know that by the beginning of April 1992, a part of the military had actually moved to Zlatiste. It was under VRS control by April 1992. You know that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your information is totally incorrect. The JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska had nothing to do with Zlatiste. The forces of the Bosnian Serbs and the police liberated Zlatiste, I think, in June or July 1992. Until that time, it was under the control of the BH army. I know that because we were unable to communicate from Lukavica via Zlatiste and Trebevic with Pale instead, we had to take the macadam road --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Zlatiste was not in our hands. You asked me about Zlatiste that was not in our hands on that April, May, 1992, let alone before that. I mean, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing to do with any of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You talked also, Mr. Tusevljak, about -- you talked about the situation in Lukavica and you had a look at some video that you said depicted some part of Grbavica. But I just want to get a couple of things straight. And that was in your testimony the last time you came here and today. I just want to get a couple of things straight. You actually, before moving to Lukavica, you actually worked in the police school in Vrace for a period, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never worked at the police school in Vrace. Only at the very beginning of the war, I was in Nedzarici, because I am from Nedzarici, and the seat of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska in April and mid-June, I think, was temporarily at the school in Vrace. And sometime in May 1992, we established a centre of security services of the Romanija and Birac area and that's where I worked, and its seat was in Vrace for perhaps about five days, because Vrace was under constant fire, artillery and infantry fire. We had many casualties, many people wounded, killed. The conditions were simply not right for work and, therefore, on the basis of an order of the minister of the interior, we withdrew to --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I just asked you whether or not you worked there. Your answer was for a period of time temporarily, perhaps for about five days. Now I just want to stay with that area of town because you said in your testimony in-chief I was in Grbavica very often during the war. So let's stay with that area of town because I want to know what you would have seen being in Grbavica. You would have seen the mortars in that area of town. Grbavica isn't a big place. So you would have seen them; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never saw mortars in Grbavica. And I don't know of any -- I wasn't at the actual front line but as far as I know in this civilian area because I also lived in Grbavica, I had a refugee apartment there, and that was the reason why I was there for a while, while the centre was in Lukavica. That's why I was in Grbavica. And I never saw any mortars in Grbavica. I'm now talking about the residential urban area of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see the APCs, the APCs on Ozrenska street in the immediate vicinity of the police school? Did you see the APCs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? May? When? Well, of course, we had police APCs and the military had their own. And the command was there, the army command. This is normal military weaponry. I saw tanks too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where did you see the tanks in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about Ozrenska street now. The difference between Ozrenska and Grbavica is perhaps a kilometre as the crow flies and if you take a vehicle, it's 3 or 4 kilometres. You should know the configuration of the terrain. This really has nothing to do with one another. Grbavica -- I mean, do you know what a tank would be in Grbavica? I mean, it's like this. It would have been destroyed with a Zolja or Osa, the same second because it was visible this way from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tanks? That's all I asked?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the periphery now, Ozrenska, I don't know. Zagorska, and so on. I mean, the names of those streets, well, in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In all fairness to the witness [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... where is the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where he did see the tanks in Grbavica. At the same time, I establish that he started talking about tanks where you had asked only about APCs. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would have seen the sharpshooters; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see any sharpshooters for the reasons that I have already mentioned. Namely, I wasn't at the front line itself. Believe me, I absolutely did not. How could I see a sharpshooter? If there are any sharpshooters, they're at the very front line. They're not way back at the fifth line. What did I see? Somebody sniping, carrying a sniper rifle? What?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, you haven't seen them. That's what you were asked for. Whether you could have seen them, or where they were there, whether they should be close to the lines or not is not something that was asked. You haven't seen it; you've answered the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you were in Grbavica so much during the course of the war, you know what the Serb army firing positions were. Don't you? Because they were in the immediate vicinity of the police school, among other places.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you talk to witnesses, I do apologise, a map would suffice and then the Trial Chamber can be shown very clearly where the police school is, where the Serb line is, where the Bosniak line is. Because the MUP school is in Vrace. It's not at Grbavica. I know -- I mean, if you didn't know at that time in Grbavica where the front lines were and where the sniping was, you'd be dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll give you a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32903c which is a cutout from 65 ter number 32903 with the operative date of 19 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tusevljak, this map depicts part of Grbavica, depicts Grbavica and part of Vrace. It shows tanks moving along the road immediately behind the police school and you see the police school marked just near the stadium. And it shows tanks, APCs and machine-guns throughout Grbavica and Vrace. So you asked for the map.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the date of this map? Where were these tanks marked? Which date? Which year?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've already said 1992 December. So, Mr. Tusevljak, your evidence is that you didn't see any of the combat equipment that was deployed throughout Grbavica and Vrace, except for the tanks and the APCs; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is December 1992. In the school at Vrace in December 1992 there was not a single policemen. So the school in Vrace was completely abandoned. It was at the actual front line. My communication with Grbavica went along the road from Lukavica, then I went down this road, you see here? The one that's been marked here? Towards Milavici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, please. Then the road that goes down to Grbavica, it's that road. That's where there was a sniper shooting all the time and it was visible from Sarajevo all the time. I had no need to go right or left anywhere because I did not belong to the Army of Republika Srpska so there was no need for me to go to the front line itself. Just take a look at this road. Just take a look at this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you could do yourself a favour, you have testified here three times now, and you know how difficult it is for the interpreters to accurately interpret what you say when you speak at such speed and when you don't make a pause between your sentences. So I'm sorry to have had to speak so to you, but it causes the interpreters difficulty to do their job when you speak so quickly. If I could just encourage you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do apologise to the interpreters. But, quite simply, I get carried away. I'm going to repeat this, if it's not too hard. In December --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... would you like to mark something on the map, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about the journey I took where the police station was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that -- we're getting away from the question that I asked before we go further and I need to clarify this for my own sake. Your -- is your evidence that, apart from the tanks and the APCs you've mentioned, you didn't see the combat equipment and the mortars that this map shows deployed in Grbavica and Vrace?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see them. I've already told you actually when I was talking about the first time it was April and May when I said that I saw APCs and tanks. This is a map from the month of December. By then, my headquarters was in Lukavica and I only went to my apartment or the police station and it's this road here. I can mark it for you: From Lukavica to Grbavica through Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I'm okay with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution Exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32903C receives exhibit number P7522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we decide on admission you say it's a extract were another 65 ter, which means not in evidence otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct, it is not. It's 65 ter 32903. Which is a map of the units of the 1st Corps and the District Staff of the defence of Sarajevo dated 19 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That most likely is a very large map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it not be good nevertheless to know what this is an extract of and to have that or the text, even if it has no printout for us, but to even have an opportunity to look at it in e-court. Because then if you'd then have the extract uploaded together with the whole of the map, then at least we have an opportunity to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it will be marked for identification, P7522, awaiting uploading the large map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of my colleagues suggests that we -- we could already admit this extract and then that you separately upload the whole of it but I saw that you received further instructions as well so as I did. Could you convey them to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, I'm advised that the large map is already uploaded with an English translation of the texts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P7522 is admitted into evidence and do you went then to tender the fully uploaded -- the entire map with English text and that would be under number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was - let me just -

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32903.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes under that number. Then P7523 is admitted into evidence, being the entire map. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I just want to talk about Lukavica for a second. You actually moved to Energoinvest in Lukavica sometime during the summer of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the witness properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you say Energoinvest that's actually a really huge complex, isn't it, and it's less than about 2 kilometres southeast of Lukavica. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know how you imagine Lukavica to be, but Energoinvest being in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll show you another map and with can we look at 65 ter 32903B, please. It's another cutout of the same map we've just admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be some confusion. If you first ask whether the witness moved to Energoinvest in Lukavica, and then later say that Energoinvest is 2 kilometres from Lukavica, that's confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed, I was referring to the barracks which is why I thought rather than speak I could clarify my situation with a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, we have another cutout from the Lukavica area of the map that we just spoke about, and if you still remember how to use the markers in e-court for e-court, I'd like you to just draw a circle around Energoinvest where your office was in Lukavica. If it's difficult for you, if you look in the middle of the page you see Electrotechnical Faculty written and then you see to the right of that, Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has marked a circle with the location of his office at Lukavica for whatever period of time he stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is not very clear. I think it is just a little bit up from where the map reads Electrotechnical Faculty just slightly to the right, slightly above, there's a very small, red, small circle. That's the what the witness marked. Ms. Edgerton, now knowing what the witness marked, wouldn't that be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. If I could please have this as another Prosecution Exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked map receives exhibit number P7524.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7524 is admitted into evidence. Witness, you may follow the usher. We'll take a break and would like to see you back at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I, a few times, I urged the witness that there was no need to tell us why he didn't know something, but you're triggering that by your questions, by including in your questions why he should know. So if you first asked what he knows and then depending on the answer, of course, you could further inquire. But this triggers, again and again, long explanations as why the witness thinks he should not know or that was not logical, but you're triggering it yourself, and I'd like to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, to go onto another area, I just want to talk about how you got your information. Because in your examination-in-chief, at transcript page 38460, when you were discussing shelling on Serb-held areas, my friend asked how you came to this information and you said two things. You said you were informed about it by members of the army and you also know about these locations because persons of Serb ethnicity who came to Ilidza from these areas and who were interviewed indicated the locations from which the firing was coming. So with that reminder in place, I'd just like that ask you: Can you tell us when exactly your office moved from Lukavica to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office moved, I think, in March 1994. However, from March until September, during that period of time, I worked at the seat of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska in Bijeljina and then from the 1st of September, 1994, I returned to Ilidza yet again, where the seat of the centre was, and I continued doing the same work, chief of department for the crime prevention police. So September 1994 until the end of war, I was in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the people, the line crossers, the refugees, the people who escaped, the people that you referred to who crossed the line to Serb-held territory and gave information to your colleagues and your team in the police would have told you about the situation that they were living in, in Bosnian-held territory; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they gave statements, and that is one of the ways in which information was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So they would told you -- you spoke about Hrasnica in your evidence in-chief. So they would have told you about the situation for civilians in Hrasnica. That's how you got your information; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They spoke about their suffering and the suffering of others that they had been aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And they would have told you, for example, about Hrasnica being shelled; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that kind of question was not put to them. What they talked about was their suffering, and we got the statements of the military security. And, in those statements, there were references to positions of enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying -- because you had talked earlier about your team and your team going to do on-site investigations. You're saying you didn't receive information about the situation for civilians from your team?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the supervisor then, and my colleagues interviewed these persons and, of course, these interviews and statements were accessible to me. There's an official report that was written up by one of my operatives, and then I would have to read it whether there was enough information there. I was not the signatory of the official report, but I had to make it known to my supervisors by placing my initials there that I had read these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right then. Did you read reports about the civilian population in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the suffering of Serbs in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at P6756, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to that and before looking at it, you said shelling of Hrasnica was not what they were asked about. Did you consider that -- let's just for argument's sake assume that there was -- some shells were fired at Hrasnica, you didn't consider that to be part of the suffering of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm telling you we did not talk to them then. I mean, we talked about the suffering of the civilian population with persons who were leaving Hrasnica. We did not talk to them about shelling from Serb positions. I mean, we didn't. I mean, it wasn't the topic of our conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still do not understand. I mean, are you saying we didn't ask them because never any shell was fired at Hrasnica, or do you say being shelled is not part of suffering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shelling was part of suffering, but it wasn't only these people from Hrasnica. Any other witnesses. That's not what was discussed with them. If they had been detained, what was discussed was how they were treated, whether they witnessed killings and other forms of torture. Whereas, the military security talked to them about that topic, from where the enemy fired at Ilidza, Vojkovici, Nedzarici. So that's for that area, and others, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before you call up that document, just to ask further about your sources of information, you said the military security talked to them. Parts of your team talked to them. Who else talked to them? What were your sources of information from civilians who were leaving Sarajevo? Who did you get the information from?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information from my employees whose job it was to talk to these civilians about war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what kind of liaison did you have with, for example, your own security services?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With members of the Ministry of Interior, horizontally and vertically. We were in communication every day. These people worked on the same floor as I.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so sharing information about the security situation would have been a normal procedure for you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discuss the security situation. Crime prevention police investigates crimes. There is a National Security Service. There was at that time within the Ministry of Interior. There is military security within the Army of Republika Srpska. We belonged to the public security. Crime prevention police investigates criminal offences and in that period, 1994/1995, we also investigated war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So let's have a look at - and not for broadcast, please - P6756. So this is a report from the SNB Ilidza about the situation in Hrasnica from a very reliable source. And it says in the third full paragraph: "Hrasnica is shelled the hardest from the direction of Gavric Brdo, Gornji Kotorac, Vojkovici and Igman and it was reported that shells occasionally also fly in from Igman mountain, due to misfire of Muslim artillery. According to the Muslim authorities in Hrasnica, since the beginning of the war shelling by Serbian forces caused severe to light injuries to 3.000 persons. In that area, there are currently 5.500 children." Is this a crime that you would have investigated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that is an Official Note from the National Security Service, the department in Ilidza. The date is 6 May 1993 when I was still in Lukavica, and this is the first time I see this Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is the shelling by Serbian forces that caused severe to light injuries to 3.000 persons something you would have investigated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if I read it well - and I think in all fairness to the witness it should be clear to him as well - that what we see under these bullet points is proceeded by a text saying the following information was published through the newspapers in Sarajevo whereas you introduced this material as a type of information you would receive from people who crossed the lines, whereas it seems to be newspaper sources rather than anything else, and I think would be fair to the witness that you make that clear to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see on top of the first bullet, Mr. Tusevljak, that the following information was published, through the newspapers in Sarajevo. You've seen that in your own language. So that's what I am reading to you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are obviously trying to deceive me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is pure deceit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, would you refrain from expressing accusations. Rather, answer the question. Please proceed when answering the question and refrain from comments as you just made a second ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is evident now, Muslim forces placed this information, which is false, for news publishing houses in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This translation into English is not quite correct. For this sentence at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, we are also now informed that the translation is perhaps not fully correct. Witness, would be please so kind and I know that this is usually not done but since I received this comment, could you read the line which is the first line of the paragraph where the bullet points are think it starts with "za novinarske kuce [B/C/S spoken]." Could you read that line for us slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The following information has been provided to the news publishing houses in Sarajevo. The area of Hrasnica has an excellently organised hospital" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited you had to read the first line primarily. Now you earlier commented on who had provided this. And do you have any knowledge about that? Because you say that you for the first time see all this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's all I can read from this Official Note written by (redacted) But it's obvious that this information was provided by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that name of the (redacted) because he was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we should have a redaction there. Witness, I'm -- one second. In the ... You said: "It is evident now Muslim forces placed this information, which is false, for news publishing houses in Sarajevo." Could you tell us what you know as to who provided this information to the publishing houses in Sarajevo? If you have any knowledge. If you don't have any knowledge, then please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within their Supreme Command, there was a special Department for Liaison -- for public relations and you will see from statements and I've read hundreds of them, of the Bosnian army members and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not interested in general as to who provided information, both for this information, where you said it's evident now, Muslim forces placed this information. Do you have as any specific knowledge as who provided this information which is contained in this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this Official Note, I cannot see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you dispute that -- just having heard your comment with respect to this document. Is it your position that residential buildings in areas of Hrasnica were not shelled by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information. I was not a member of the army, nor did I have occasion to look where shells were falling in Hrasnica, if any. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have one small follow-up question. You say the information is false and now asked about any shells fired at Hrasnica, you say, I don't know it. Does that mean that at least on that issue, you can't tell us whether this information is false or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the author of the text says that information was placed, that verb, "placed," is used to denote that some information was given to someone trying to present it as the truth. If the meaning were different, the language would be different. It would read, for instance, according to information or according to reports, et cetera. That's the difference in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those are your conclusions, but you're still unable to tell us whether information about the shelling of Hrasnica was false or was not false?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Hrasnica and also on the boundary towards the combat zone in Ilidza there were Muslim units and their commends that were certainly shelled. I can confirm that. It was a war zone on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A minute ago you said you had no knowledge about that. But let's leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in the information you received from people who had fled or escaped or been exchanged or otherwise left Bosnian-held territory, Bosnian-held Sarajevo, did you receive reports of shelling by VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in those reports, I did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now you've just commented on something that (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Redaction, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just commented on one of your police colleagues had drafted on the basis of information received. You've indicated that you received information from the military and from your own team. Is it your evidence that you received in your intel interviews no information about shelling of Bosnian-held Sarajevo from these line-crossers and people who were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said we did not conduct intel interviews. We took statements on specific incidents of war crime and all the statements taken from these persons in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure from that time were submitted to the prosecutor. The reason we interviewed these people was to get information about cases of war crimes and to provide that information to the prosecution. The crime prevention police did not have for a purpose to obtain any intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so nobody told you that they couldn't give information about cases of war crimes within your mandate because they were too afraid to go outside? Nobody told you that the shelling of Bosnian-held Sarajevo by VRS forces kept them inside their homes, scared, too afraid to go out, and they couldn't give any of the information you were after?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Nobody gave me that as a reason. And in the books of the mortuary of the Kosevo Hospital that we reviewed there are Serb victims whose cause of death is not indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the break is in just a couple of minutes and I would actually go to another area now, so maybe it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we should not do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning because we are not able to conclude your testimony today. I instruct you again that you should not speak or communicate in of what way with whomever about your testimony, whether that's testimony you've given either in July or last week, or this week, or still to be given tomorrow. If you understand this instruction, then you may now follow the usher and we see back you tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, before we break you put to the witness that he received military information and there was no objection by Mr. Lukic but, of course, the witness clearly said that the military security talked to those who had crossed the lines about that topic from where the enemy fired at Ilidza. So it was apparently not part of what the witness's team discussed with the crossers. But to the extent you suggest it that his answer would have included that the military did that, the witness had clearly answered that the military was interested in the enemy firing at Ilidza, not in any firing at Hrasnica from where the crossers came. So I want to urge you to be very precise in not misstating or even suggesting that that was something that the witness has said. We -- before we adjourn, could you tell us approximately where you in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The estimate is that I have an hour and a half of my estimated time left, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another matter, and I'm also addressing you, Mr. Lukic, if the Chamber understood your cross-examination well that it was very much until now on the lists, et cetera, was focussing not on exactly what happened with A, B or C but rather the reliability of the information contained in that lest and there's no dispute about Serbs falling victim of -- and Mr. Lukic I would like to ask you what your estimate would be as to how much time you would need, but also keep this in mind that it's not ultimately to establish this Mr. A, B or C were not victims, and apparently there's an acceptance that there were quite a number of victims, I take it, and I see Ms. Edgerton is nodding yes. So, therefore, it's mainly about reliability. Could you give us as indication as to what time you need as matters stand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Probably an hour. Which then might result in an early adjournment tomorrow, if it's true that we need altogether two and a half hours. We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 1st of September, 9.30 in the morning, this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of September, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
